newsitem.title: USA: Clinton administration to tighten wetlands rules.
newsitem.headline: Clinton administration to tighten wetlands rules.

text.p: The Clinton administration Wednesday said it will phase out rules that have allowed thousands of small wetlands areas to be drained without detailed government review.
The Army Corp of Engineers said effective February 11, it will have tighter constraints on permits it issues to fill isolated wetlands in upland areas near headwaters of streams.
It also will require that permits for those wetlands of three acres and more get the more intensive review now required for 10 acres or more.
Wetlands of one-third to three acres would get a shorter review, similar to current requirements for wetlands of one to ten acres, a Corp official said.

After two years, the Corp will replace the special permitting process, called Permit 26, with another permitting system in which the Corp would tailor permits based on the kind of activity to be done, said John Sudt, the Army Corp's chief regulatory officer.
"The intent is to reduce the degree of wetlands loss, but also to put in several of the nationwide permits restrictions to ensure that water quality is better protected," Sudt said.
Sudt said the Corp estimated that in 1996, total acreage affected by the permits was about 9,000 acres.

An estimated 105 million acres of wetlands remain in the lower 48 states, including the coastal areas and large wetlands systems not affected by this type of permit. About half the nation's wetlands -- essential for wildlife habitat, flood control and to purify water -- have been lost to development.
Environmentalists said the change will increase protections for tens of thousands of acres of wetlands across the country.

"The first thing we need to observe is this is an important step forward, but they're not not going far enough and they're not going fast enough," said Drew Caputo, of the Natural Resources Defence Council.

The Permit 26 programme, a process started during the Reagan administration to allow fast-track reviews of wetlands permits, has long been blasted by environmentalists as a green light to developers to fill and drain wetlands with scant or no review, and to target their projects to fall just under the permits' limits to escape interference.
The small isolated parcels add up to thousands of acres per year, and can make a huge difference in wildlife habitat and water quality, they say.
Caputo said the Corp should move faster than the two year transition which he said will allow thousands of wetlands to be filled.

Also, he said, while the Corp must be notified of plans to fill wetlands as small as one-third to one acre, it does not have to pass the information onto other agencies such as the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service where calls for more protections often originate.

But Caputo said the eventual move to activity specific permits "is the right solution because will be able to set limits on activities that harm the wetlands" provided the Corp writes the permits responsibly.
